normalization_or_editorial_flags.issue: ce que je pense normally reads 'what I think'; English 'what I'm thinking' is closer to ce que je suis en train de penser. Rank 754 is the exact progressive variant.
je vous/te prie is formal or dated relative to the surrounding contemporary learner register; simplify during native editorial review.
Je ne sais ce que... without pas is literary/formal; keep only if elevated register is intentionally represented.
French says 'indicate the nearest bus stop'; English asks where it is. Semantically sound but not structurally exact.
manger là is grammatical but less idiomatic than y manger in this context; the paired y variants are cleaner.
French asks how long the listener waited; English adds 'had to wait'. Tighten obligation nuance if exact equivalence is required.
English ends with 'thinking about' while French says simply ce que nous pensons; English itself is slightly awkward and should be normalized.
de quoi il s'agit maps to what this is about; English 'what this is all about' adds emphasis. Acceptable but can be aligned more tightly.
répéter/redire are being used for 'tell me again'; some are natural, some are slightly awkward. Standardize repeated-request phrasing during second pass.
tirer de mon rein is understandable for 'get for my kidney' but the subject matter and phrasing should receive native-register review before inclusion in a general learner workbook.
Subjunctive choices in interrogative/relative constructions are plausible but should be normalized by a native editor rather than mechanically changed.
Conversational word order is valid spoken French but mixed with formal inversion; retain only under an explicit mixed-register policy.
French existential wording and English progressive wording are close but not aspect-identical; review exact standalone equivalence.
Qui êtes-vous pour... is idiomatically close to 'Who do you think you are to...'; decide whether exact wording matters for the learner pair.
prier quelqu'un de is formal and English 'have him call' is more neutral/causative; native-register review recommended.
Subjunctive after la dernière chose que is defensible; normalize only through native editorial review.
French vous is ambiguous between polite singular and plural, while English explicitly says 'you guys'; prefer an unambiguously plural French context for standalone learning.
Connaissez-vous quelqu'un... means 'Do you know anyone...'; English says 'Do you have anyone...'. Pragmatically close but not literal.
Normalize spacing before the final question mark after 21 heures.
bon à rien / naze / se mettre en quatre vary substantially in register; keep only with deliberate register labeling or replace with more neutral learner material.
